synopsis: As of October 2026, the booklet treats human factors as essential to heavy off-road collision-mitigation validation: coverage must include warning meaning, habituation, reaction time, predictable escalation and restart, while operator and pedestrian models require their own validation [f2957, f2924, f10350]. Acceptance is a material operational risk: 2024 mining research links false-positive interventions to production losses, wear and operator resistance; workers at seven coal mines reported unnecessary shutdowns from once daily to 15 times per cut, and nearly 70% worried about how and when proximity systems take control [f1530, f3013, f11660]. The booklet recommends measuring unwanted warnings and interventions by operating hour and task rather than per detection, because an excellent aggregate false-positive rate can conceal an intervention during nearly every loading cycle; no published operator-accepted false-alarm rate was found [f11608, f11609, f248]. Evidence remains incomplete: searches found no validated off-road operator model, reaction distributions or study quantifying the change from warning-only to automatic braking, so current fleet behavior may not predict future reliance, reactions or overrides [f250, f3042, f7482, f7479, f7480]. Human-in-the-loop evidence may be needed for operator-response claims, but simulator studies cannot establish long-term trust, complacency or production-pressure effects, and independently validated perception and braking components do not establish closed-loop safety [f8208, f961, f8196].
